causal_questions.question: Why did the Aeolus-Clover planned outage leave the Wyoming area vulnerable to cascading after switching proceeded?
causal_questions.answer: PACE removed the Aeolus-Clover line from service after no violations were identified, but the system was actually in an unidentified N-1 insecure state. Before switching, PACE raised the Aeolus RAS arming setpoints above actual flow, effectively disarming the RAS for current conditions, and no wind reductions were taken.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence directly supports a candidate root-cause chain: insecure state not identified, RAS effectively disarmed, and no wind reduction before switching.

causal_questions.question: What specific planned transmission action initiated the November 13 Wyoming disturbance?
causal_questions.answer: The disturbance was triggered by the planned outage/removal from service of a single 500 kV transmission line. The report identifies that line as the PacifiCorp East Aeolus-Clover 500 kV line.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence is strong for the initiating action and line identity.

causal_questions.question: How did the disturbance propagate after the Aeolus-Clover line was lost?
causal_questions.answer: Flows shifted onto the Aeolus-Anticline line, causing local voltage to collapse to 138 kV. Protective relaying then tripped the Aeolus-Anticline line within 0.4 seconds, and within 6 seconds an electrical island formed and collapsed while frequency dropped and underfrequency load shedding activated.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence directly describes the propagation sequence from flow shift to voltage collapse, relay trip, island collapse, and frequency/load-shedding response.

causal_questions.question: What customer, load, and generation impacts resulted from the cascading outage?
causal_questions.answer: The disturbance caused cascading line outages affecting approximately 250,000 customers, with outages lasting up to 9.5 hours in some areas. It also resulted in the loss of more than 4,800 MW of generation, and customers in PACE, BHE, Tri-State G&T, and WACM lost power for hours, with some industrial customers out until the next day.
causal_questions.notes: Evidence directly supports the high-level customer duration, generation-loss, and affected-entity impacts.

causal_questions.question: What mitigation actions or needed operating adjustments did the report describe around the overlapping outages and restoration?
causal_questions.answer: Before the event, studies by SPP, RCW, and WACM indicated that additional PACE wind-generation reductions were needed, and RCW estimated about 820 MW of wind reduction would support both outages. After the event, affected entities began restoration processes that included mitigation of multiple N-1 contingencies, although restoration was complicated by high voltages, large phase angles, and inadequate communication.
causal_questions.notes: Candidate combines pre-event operating mitigation identified by studies with post-event restoration mitigation described in the available sentence set.

sentences.text: <Public> November 13 Wyoming Disturbance A Collaboration between WECC and NERC June 8, 2026 E LECTRIC R ELIABILITY AND S ECURITY FOR THE W EST <Public> Executive Summary On November 13, 2025, at 1243 hrs.1, the northeast region of the Western Interconnection (WI) experienced a significant system disturbance that resulted in cascading line outages and affected approximately 250,000 customers, lasting up to 9.5 hours in some areas.
The Montana–Alberta Tie Line (MATL) — WECC Path 83 — also tripped during this event.
The disturbance was triggered by a planned outage of a single 500 kV transmission line, but multiple factors exacerbated the situation, contributing to the widespread outage.
The line that was scheduled to be out of service was the PacifiCorp East (PACE) Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line.
This line, along with the Aeolus–Anticline 500 kV line, transfers large amounts of wind and thermal generation in this region to load centers across the interconnection.
The Aeolus lines require close monitoring, and outages may necessitate limiting wind generation in the area.
To ensure reliable operation, PACE implemented a Remedial Action Scheme (RAS)2 that automatically trips wind generation for outages of the 500 kV Aeolus lines, preventing broader system disturbances.
The outage of this line was planned for November 13 at 0800 in accordance with established PACE and RCW processes.

RCW and SPP had previously coordinated and agreed that the outage of the Western Area Power Administration-Rocky Mountain Region (WACM) and the outage of the Miracle Mile-Alcova west 115 kV line would not be allowed to overlap.
As the morning passed, wind generation increased in the area, which increased the amount of energy flowing across the two Aeolus 500 kV lines.

A scheme designed to detect predetermined System conditions and automatically take corrective actions that may include adjusting or tripping generation (MW and Mvar), tripping load, or reconfiguring a System(s).
Real-Time Contingency Analysis (RTCA) evaluates system conditions, such as load, generation, and transmission outages, using real-time data to assess both current and future operating conditions.

N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 1 <Public> With no violations identified, PACE removed the Aeolus–Clover line from service, operating the system in an unidentified Normal-1 (N-1)4 insecure state, which resulted in a cascading outage.
This cascading was due to a shift of flows onto the Aeolus–Anticline line, which caused the local voltage to collapse to 138 kV (~0.28 pu)5.
As designed, protective relaying tripped the Aeolus–Anticline line within 0.4 seconds of the initial loss of the Aeolus–Clover line.
While most of the WI remained functional, the disturbance culminated in the loss of more than 4,800 MW of generation from coal, natural gas, photovoltaic, and wind resources.
Within 6 seconds, an electrical island formed and collapsed, causing widespread effects across that portion of the interconnection.
The Aeolus RAS did not trip any generation because its setpoint had been raised before switching.

The resulting generation-load imbalance caused the WI frequency to drop to 59.758 Hz before recovering to 60 Hz within approximately 6 minutes, and underfrequency load shedding was activated in the northeastern region before the island collapse.

In terms of system voltages, 500 kV voltages ranged from a nominal value of approximately 520 kV (~1.0 pu) to lows of 138 kV (~0.28 pu) during the initiating part of the event and before system separation.
Due to the rapid progression of this event, no manual corrective actions were able to be taken during the trip.

As a result of this cascading outage, customers in PACE, BHE, Tri-State G&T (TSGT), and WACM lost power for hours, with some industrial load customers remaining out of service until the following day.
PACE lost 411.1 MW of firm load, affecting approximately 54,000 customers.
WACM lost 709 MW of firm load in its Balancing Authority Area (BAA), affecting approximately 47,000 sub-BA customers.

It also included: o 538 MW of firm load in BHE, affecting approximately 154,000 customers o 6.64 MW of firm load in TSGT, affecting approximately 1,900 customers Although wind generation was substantial at the time of the event, it was not identified as a contributing factor.
Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been implicated in other disturbance events6.
The IBRs in eastern Wyoming tripped appropriately for the over-/under-voltage and frequency conditions of the event.

In addition, IBRs supported a faster frequency recovery across the interconnection, driven largely by battery energy storage systems, while wind generation provided readily available capacity during system restoration.

A secure state is a condition where the power system is operating within all design constraints and can withstand the unexpected failure of any single key component — such as a transmission line, transformer, or generator — without violating security limits or causing a service interruption.
Per unit (pu) converts actual volts to a dimensionless fraction, where 1.0 pu typically represents the nominal or rated voltage.

Inverter-Based Resource Disturbances in the Western Interconnection ; October 2025 N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 2 <Public> After the event, the affected entities began their respective restoration processes.

Restoration efforts included mitigation of multiple N-1 contingencies, difficulties caused by high voltage levels, large phase angles, and inadequate communication, which resulted in instances of equipment energization between TOPs across the RC seams with no prior communication.
One thermal generation facility took over four days to recover, with one additional generator remaining out of service due to significant damage that occurred during restoration.

N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 3 <Public> • RTCA for one entity used inaccurate modeling parameters, such as operating limits and generating resource reactive capability, and had disabled alarming functions for low voltages.

N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 4 <Public> Table of Contents N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 5 <Public> N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 6 <Public> Introduction On November 13, 2025, a disturbance occurred when a planned outage of a 500 kV transmission line resulted in uncontrolled, widespread outages across the northeastern region of the Western Interconnection (WI).
To understand the underlying causes and contributing factors, WECC and NERC partnered with the stakeholders involved to conduct a comprehensive analysis.
This report contains details of the disturbance, the contributing factors identified through the analysis, and the resulting considerations.
One of the primary goals of the reliable operation8 of the Bulk Electric System (BES)9 is preventing cascading outages.
NERC defines cascading as “The uncontrolled successive loss of System Elements triggered by an incident at any location.

This excess energy is transmitted through an extensive network of long, high-voltage transmission lines to load centers throughout the To aid in transmission of this generation, PacifiCorp East (PACE) built its Energy Gateway project10.
This event occurred in November, a shoulder month, when a significant amount of maintenance is performed on BES lines and equipment.

Operating the elements of the BPS within equipment and electric system thermal, voltage, and stability limits so instability, uncontrolled separation, or cascading failures of the system will not occur as a result of a sudden disturbance, including a cybersecurity incident or unanticipated failure of system elements.
Transmission elements operated at 100 kV or higher and real power and reactive power resources connected at 100 kV or higher.
Pre-Disturbance Conditions On November 12, 2025, the day before the disturbance, several transmission lines in this region were already out of service for maintenance, as shown in Figure 2.

On November 13, during its regular morning conference call, RCW acknowledged the PACE Aeolus– Clover line outage while SPP identified another scheduled outage for the day: that of the Western Area Power Administration — Rocky Mountain Region (WACM) Alcova–Miracle Mile 115 kV West line.
The Aeolus–Clover line outage was planned to facilitate the return to service of Little Snake Reactor #1 and to remove Coyote Reactor #2 from service.
Following the switching of the reactors, the Aeolus–Clover line would be returned to service, and the Coyote Reactor #2 would remain out of service with a scheduled return on November 19, 2025.
The PACE Grid Operator East (GOE) started switching for the outage of the Aeolus–Clover line at 0800 hrs., effectively bypassing the series capacitors at Coyote substation.
Switching personnel were not scheduled to be at Little Snake substation until later due to the scheduled noon end time of the outage of Little Snake Reactor #1.
Due to the delay in the line switching, the PACE GOE re-inserted the series capacitors at Coyote substation.

SPP identified in its Real-time Assessment (RTA)13 studies that the simultaneous outages of the Aeolus–Clover line and the Miracle Mile West main bus would require mitigation plans to maintain the reliable operation of the BES.
SPP informed WACM that there was not a good mitigation plan to support overlapping the outage of their Miracle Mile West main bus and PACE Aeolus–Clover 500 kV line.
SPP also informed RCW that studies with the overlapping outages showed overloads up to 130% on the remaining Alcova–Miracle Mile East 115 kV line, even with assuming activation of the Aeolus RAS.

Due to these study results involving outages across the RC seam, SPP would not allow the outages to overlap and notified WACM that it could not proceed with the Miracle Mile outage until the Aeolus–Clover line was returned to service.

RCW notified SPP that the Aeolus–Clover line outage was delayed for 3 hours due to the absence of a switching personnel scheduled at Little Snake until noon, when the line was originally planned to be returned to service.
RCW also indicated that if WACM would like to proceed with its Miracle Mile West main bus outage, PACE agreed to limit its wind as needed to mitigate any overloads.
WACM proceeded to switch the Miracle Mile West main bus at 0950 hrs. with a scheduled return time of 1700 hrs. and included the Alcova–Miracle Mile West 115 kV line.
During the outage, as anticipated, increased loading was observed on the remaining Alcova–Miracle Mile East line.

As the area generation increased, and the start time of the PACE Aeolus–Clover line outage approached, the RCs and utilities studied what system adjustments would be needed to accommodate both outages.
SPPs studies showed loading of 138% on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line for loss of the PACE Aeolus–Anticline line.
N OVEMBER 13 W YOMING D ISTURBANCE 10 <Public> potential PACE wind reductions if both the Aeolus–Clover line and the Miracle Mile bus outages occurred simultaneously.
Their study identified that about 400 MW of wind reduction would be needed to mitigate the loading on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line.

WACM studies showed that if the Aeolus–Clover line was removed from service, the loading would increase to over 130% with the next contingent loss of the Dave Johnston–Goshen 230 kV line, even with the 400 MW of previously identified wind reductions.

SPP informed RCW of significant reliability concerns on the WACM Alcova–Miracle Mile East line loading if overlapped with the PACE outage, and use of area phase-shifters would not be enough to mitigate the exceedances.
Studies conducted by SPP, RCW, and WACM all indicated the need for additional reductions to PACE wind generation in the area.
RCW’s analysis showed that approximately 820 MW of wind would need to be reduced, bringing output down to about 2,500 MW, to support both outages.
The RCs discussed relaying this information to PACE to determine whether it would begin reducing wind generation before the planned 500 kV line outage.

RCW discussed with PACE the possibility of overlapping the outages with WACM and stated that its studies indicated a need for a wind-generation reduction of 820 MW from the current 3,300 MW level, including the specific locations where generation was reduced in the analysis.
SPP later informed RCW that WACM was evaluating the proposed 820 MW PACE wind reduction.
RCW notified PACE that it was seeing loading over 125% on the Alcova–Miracle Mile East line for loss of the Aeolus–Clover line and asked whether PACE could complete its wind reduction.

PACE was delaying the wind reduction due to a massive telecommunications outage that was affecting its ability to raise generation outside the Wyoming area to compensate for the reduction of wind generation.
At this time RCW and PACE agreed to a 200 MW reduction in wind generation.
RCW confirmed that PACE still wanted to take the Aeolus–Clover line outage and that it was seeing no issues with taking the outage.
RCW notified PACE that the Miracle Mile bus had returned to service and that PACE could hold off on the wind reductions currently in progress.
Due to the communications outage, the PACE shift supervisor took over switching from the PACE GOE.
Aeolus RAS Protocol In preparation for the Aeolus–Clover line outage, PACE raised the Aeolus RAS arming setpoints above the current actual flow16.
This effectively disarmed the RAS for the current conditions and prevented any trips from being sent to generation facilities if a monitored piece of equipment tripped or was taken out of service.
PACE would then use the amount of generation reduced in the contingency analysis as the amount of generation reduction needed before switching.
In this instance, it identified no issues in the contingency analysis, and so took no reductions in the wind, and the RAS was left in this adjusted status.

The next real-time contingency analysis (RTCA) scan, after the Aeolus RAS setpoints were adjusted to enable switching, started showing low voltage results, specifically in the Aeolus and Anticline areas.
